about.title: Richmond Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: A hospital stay or clinic visit in Richmond is supposed to leave you better off, not worse. When it doesn't, the hard part is knowing whether what happened was an unavoidable complication or a genuine breach of the standard of care. California law draws that line clearly: a bad result by itself is not malpractice. What matters is whether a reasonably careful provider would have acted differently, and proving that almost always takes a qualified medical expert reviewing your records. Richmond residents seeking care across Contra Costa County also face MICRA's timelines. In most cases you have one year from the day you discovered the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself, with a 90-day notice sent to the provider before any suit is filed. Those windows close quietly. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects you with an independent attorney who handles malpractice matters on contingency, so the review costs you nothing up front and there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: My injury was missed in a Richmond emergency room after a crash on I-80. Is that malpractice?
items.answer: It can be, but not automatically. Richmond recorded 618 people injured in collisions in 2025, and many were treated in busy emergency settings where some conditions are hard to spot. The question is whether a reasonably careful ER provider would have caught it given the same information. An independent attorney can have a medical expert review the chart to answer that.

items.question: How long do I have to file a malpractice claim in California?
items.answer: Under MICRA, you generally have one year from when you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury. There is also an outer limit of three years from the date of the injury itself, with narrow exceptions. Before filing, a 90-day notice of intent must be sent to the provider, so it's wise to start early.
